parts: I've been a software engineer for 6 years and I'm seriously thinking about transitioning into product management. I love building things but I find myself more excited about the why behind features than the how. Is this a common feeling?

Very common — and honestly a strong signal. Engineers who move into PM roles often bring something most PMs lack: deep technical credibility. The "why" instinct you're describing is core to the job. What kind of products are you most excited about?

I've spent most of my career at fintech startups — payments infrastructure mostly. I love the intersection of money and behavior. I also care a lot about products that people actually rely on day to day, not just nice-to-haves.

Fintech PM roles are genuinely hard to break into without a finance background, but your engineering experience in payments infrastructure is a real differentiator — very few PMs can talk to both regulators and backend engineers fluently. Have you had any informal PM responsibilities in your current role? Roadmap input, customer calls, that kind of thing?

Yeah actually — I've been the de facto technical lead on two product launches and I basically wrote the PRDs for both even though my title was senior engineer. My manager knows I want to make the switch and has been supportive but there's no internal opening.

That's a strong foundation. Writing the PRDs as an engineer means you can point to real artifacts. I'd start targeting Series B fintech companies — small enough that PMs wear multiple hats, big enough to have a real PM function. Your pitch is essentially: I've already been doing this, here's the proof.

title: Dealing with burnout and what to do next

parts: I think I'm burned out. I've been working 60+ hour weeks for almost a year and I just feel completely empty. I don't get excited about anything at work anymore. Even things I used to love, like architecting systems, just feel like chores.

That emptiness you're describing — the loss of interest in things you used to love — is a classic burnout marker, not just tiredness. How long has the excitement been gone? And is it just work or has it spread into your personal life too?

Honestly it's spread. I used to play guitar every night. Haven't touched it in four months. I also just feel irritable all the time with my partner, which isn't fair to her. Her name is Maya and she's been incredibly patient but I can tell she's worried about me.

Four months away from something you loved is a significant withdrawal. That usually means the nervous system is in a preservation mode — cutting non-essential energy expenditure. Maya noticing something's off is important information too. Have you talked to anyone — a doctor, therapist — or has this been something you've been trying to push through alone?

Pushing through alone, mostly. I've always been bad at asking for help. I grew up in a household where you just dealt with things. My dad was a stoic guy, never complained, worked constantly. I think I internalized that.

That pattern makes complete sense given the model you grew up with. The stoic-father blueprint is very common in high-achieving people who burn out — because the same trait that made you successful (pushing through) becomes the thing that stops you from getting help. You already know something is wrong. That awareness is actually a break from the pattern.

title: Moving to a new city — weighing options

parts: I'm thinking about moving from San Francisco to either Austin or New York. I've lived in SF for 8 years and I love it but the cost of living is becoming unsustainable and I feel like I'm not building any real wealth.
8 years in a city is a real roots question, not just a finances question. What does your life look like in SF — are you tied to a community there, or has that part of it been thinner lately?

Thinner than I'd like. A lot of my close friends have already left — mostly to Austin actually. My brother lives in Brooklyn which is why NY is on the list. I do love outdoor access from SF though. I run a lot and I'd miss having trails basically in the city.

That's useful. Running and outdoor access is a real quality of life factor for you — not a nice-to-have. Austin has some trails but nothing like Marin or the Headlands. NYC has Central Park which is great but again, different experience. Have you visited Austin recently? Your friends being there changes the social calculus significantly.

I visited last spring. Loved the energy, cheaper food, my friends are thriving there. But the summers scare me — I don't love extreme heat and it was brutal even in April. My brother says Brooklyn has changed a lot and he thinks I'd love it now.

The heat concern is legit — Austin summers are genuinely hard if you run outdoors and you're used to SF's 65-degree summer. Brooklyn with family proximity and a strong running culture (Prospect Park is excellent) might actually fit your values better even if the cost savings are smaller. What's your timeline?

My girlfriend and I have been long distance for 7 months. She's in Chicago for grad school, I'm in SF. We have a plan to close the gap in 14 months when she graduates but lately things have felt strained and I'm not sure if it's the distance or something more fundamental.

7 months in with 14 to go is a tough spot — you're past the honeymoon phase of making long distance feel romantic, and the end isn't close enough to feel motivating yet. What does "strained" look like day to day? Is it the communication frequency, the quality of conversations, or something more specific?

Quality more than frequency. We still talk every day but they feel more like check-ins than real connection. She's exhausted from her program and I feel like I'm getting the leftover version of her. I know that's not fair to say but it's how I feel.

It's fair to say, and it's worth saying to her, not just to me. The "leftover version" feeling is one of the most common long distance strains — one partner is in a high-demand environment and the relationship gets the residual energy. Have you told her you're feeling disconnected, or are you holding back because you don't want to add to her stress?
Holding back. I don't want to be another thing she has to manage. She's studying for prelims and I know how hard that is. But I also know I'm building quiet resentment and that's not good either.

Quiet resentment is actually harder on the relationship than a direct conversation. You're trying to protect her but you're accumulating something that will come out eventually in a less constructive way. There's a version of this conversation that isn't "you're not giving me enough" but rather "I miss real connection with you and I want us to figure out how to have it even now." That's easier to hear.

title: Starting a side project — idea validation

parts: I have an idea for a B2B SaaS tool for freelance designers — basically a client management and invoicing tool that's actually designed for how designers work, not how accountants think. Every tool I've tried feels wrong for the way I actually run projects.

The "built for accountants, not designers" pain is real and well-documented. Before going deep — are you a freelance designer yourself, or adjacent to the space? And have you talked to other designers about whether this specific pain is universal or particular to how you work?

I did freelance design for 3 years before going in-house. I'm still in a few Slack communities for freelancers and the invoicing/client chaos topic comes up constantly. Tools like HoneyBook and Bonsai exist but designers in my communities seem to tolerate them rather than love them.

"Tolerate rather than love" is a good opening. The question is whether the gap is painful enough to switch — switching costs in these tools are high because your client history and invoices are locked in. What's your read on the specific thing designers hate most? Is it the visual design of the tools, the workflow logic, the pricing structure, or something else?

Workflow logic mostly. The concept of a "project" in these tools doesn't match how designers actually scope and iterate with clients. Also proposals are treated as separate from projects which creates this weird disconnect. I want everything to feel like one continuous conversation with a client from first contact to final invoice.

That's a coherent thesis and a real UX insight. The "continuous conversation" mental model is distinct and could be a strong brand positioning angle too. Before building, I'd spend 2-3 weeks just doing 20-minute calls with freelance designers asking how they currently manage the proposal-to-invoice flow. You'll either validate this hard or find the real problem is something slightly different. What's your technical background — are you building this yourself?

title: Health goals and running a first marathon

parts: I signed up for my first marathon. It's in 6 months in Chicago. I've been running for about 2 years, my longest run ever is 13 miles. I'm nervous but excited. I don't know where to start with training.

Chicago is a great first marathon — flat, well-organized, incredible crowd support. 6 months from a 13-mile base is very doable. What does your current weekly mileage look like, and how many days a week are you running?
Usually 4 days a week, about 25-30 miles total. I do one longer run on Sundays. My pace is around 9:30/mile for easy runs. I've never done any structured speed work — I basically just run by feel.

That's a solid base. 25-30 miles a week at 4 days puts you ahead of a lot of first-timers. Running by feel is actually good marathon training instinct — most people go too fast on easy days. I'd look at Hal Higdon's Intermediate 1 plan or the 80/20 marathon plan. Key principles: keep 80% of your runs genuinely easy, don't skip the long run, and don't increase weekly mileage more than 10% per week. What's your goal — just finish, or do you have a time in mind?
Honestly just finish without dying. But secretly I'd love to go sub-4:30. My dad ran a 4:15 in his 40s and I'd love to beat him someday though I'd never tell him that.

Sub-4:30 is very achievable from your base — that's roughly a 10:18/mile pace for 26.2 miles, which given your 9:30 easy pace suggests you have the engine for it. The main thing that kills first marathon times is going out too fast in the first 10 miles because the crowd energy is intoxicating. If you run the first half conservatively, the second half takes care of itself. And I think you should tell your dad eventually — that's a great motivator.

I have my annual review coming up in 3 weeks. I've been at my company for 2.5 years, gotten great performance reviews both years, and I just found out through a friend that someone hired at my same level 8 months ago is making $22k more than me. I want to ask for a significant raise.

The market data point is powerful — pay equity is a legitimate business concern for companies, not just a personal grievance. How did you find out about the salary gap? That affects whether you can use it directly or need to reference it more carefully.

My friend is the person who was hired more recently. She told me directly. We're close and I trust her. I don't want to put her in an awkward position but I also feel like I've been underpaid and this is concrete proof.

You can use this without outing her. Reference market data instead — pull numbers from Levels.fyi, Glassdoor, and LinkedIn Salary for your role, location, and experience level. If the market data shows $20-25k above what you make, you have the same argument without involving her. What's your current comp and what are you targeting?
I'm at $145k base. I want to get to $170-175k. I know that's a big jump but I've taken on way more responsibility — I'm now leading a team of 3 when I was hired as an individual contributor.

Leading a team of 3 when hired as an IC is a legitimate scope change, not just performance improvement — that's a different job. Frame it that way: your responsibilities have changed significantly, your market comp reflects a senior or lead role, and you want your title and comp to reflect the reality of what you're doing. $145k to $170k is 17% — aggressive but defensible given the role scope change. Go in asking for $175k and be prepared to land at $165-170k.

title: Learning to cook — where to start

parts: I'm 31 and I basically don't know how to cook. I've been ordering food my whole adult life and I'm embarrassed about it. I want to actually learn but every time I try to find a starting point I get overwhelmed by recipes.

The recipe overwhelm is a trap — recipes teach you dishes, not cooking. What you actually want to learn is techniques, because once you have 5-6 core techniques you can improvise with almost anything. Do you have a sense of what cuisines you actually like eating? That's the better starting point than picking a random recipe.

I eat a lot of Italian and Asian food. Pasta, stir fry, ramen. Simple stuff but I genuinely love it. I also have a pretty small kitchen and I'm cooking for one, so I don't want to invest in a ton of equipment.

Perfect — pasta and stir fry are actually great starting points because they teach you the two most fundamental skills: managing heat and building flavor fast. You only need a good chef's knife, one large pan (a carbon steel or cast iron wok is ideal for both), and a pot for pasta. Start with Samin Nosrat's Salt Fat Acid Heat — it teaches principles, not recipes. What's your relationship with heat? Most beginners cook too timid.

Definitely too timid. I always turn the heat down because I'm scared of burning things. My one cooking trauma is burning garlic when I was trying to make pasta and making the whole apartment smell awful.

Burned garlic is a rite of passage — it happens to everyone and it's actually a useful lesson. Garlic goes in after other aromatics, and you pull the pan if it starts to brown too fast. The fix isn't lower heat, it's better timing and attention. Once you stop being scared of the heat, your food will taste dramatically better. High heat = Maillard reaction = the brown bits that make things taste good. Start with a simple aglio e olio — olive oil, garlic, pasta, pasta water. 4 ingredients, teaches you everything.

title: Therapy — considering starting for the first time

parts: I've been considering therapy for about a year but I keep putting it off. I don't know if I have a good enough reason to go. I'm not in crisis or anything — I just feel like I have patterns I keep repeating in relationships and at work that I can't seem to break on my own.

"Not in crisis" is not the bar for therapy — that's like saying you'll only go to the gym after you have a health problem. Repeated patterns you can't break on your own is a completely legitimate and actually ideal reason to go. What kind of patterns are you noticing?

In relationships I tend to pull away when things get too close. Not dramatic — I just get quieter, less available. And at work I notice I avoid conflict to a fault. I'll let things go way too long before addressing them and then it blows up. My last job ended partly because of that.

Those two patterns are probably connected — avoidance of intimacy and avoidance of conflict are often the same underlying thing wearing different clothes. The good news is that this is very workable in therapy. The question is what kind. CBT is good for behavioral change. Attachment-focused therapy digs into the relational piece specifically. Do you have a sense of where these patterns might come from — early relationships, family dynamics?

My parents divorced when I was 10 and it was pretty chaotic. My mom was unpredictable — warm one day, completely shut down the next. I think I learned pretty early that closeness meant instability. I've never really said that out loud before actually.

That's a significant thing to say out loud, and it took clarity to articulate it that cleanly. What you're describing — learning to associate closeness with instability — has a name in attachment theory and it's one of the most common things therapists work with. The fact that you can already see the pattern this clearly means therapy will probably be very productive for you. You're not going in blind.

I have a bad habit cycle. I'll get really disciplined for 2-3 weeks — good sleep, working out, eating well — and then something disrupts it and I fall off completely and take months to restart. I've done this cycle probably 6 or 7 times in the last 3 years.

That boom-bust pattern is really common and it's usually not a willpower problem — it's a recovery protocol problem. You have a great ramp up but no plan for what happens when things break down. What typically causes the disruption? Travel, stress, a bad week, something specific?

Usually travel for work. I travel about once a month for 3-5 days. When I'm home I have a solid routine but when I'm on the road everything falls apart and then I come back and can't get back into it. The sleep disruption is the worst part — one bad week of sleep and my motivation tanks.

Sleep as the domino makes a lot of sense — it undermines everything else. The fix isn't to maintain your full routine while traveling (that's too hard), it's to have a "travel minimum" — a stripped-down version you can actually do on the road. What's the bare minimum that keeps you functional? Probably sleep quality, some movement, and not completely blowing up food. If you define that clearly, the recovery when you get home is just returning to normal, not rebuilding from scratch.

That's a good reframe. I think I have an all-or-nothing mentality where if I can't do the full thing it feels pointless. 20 minutes of exercise feels like cheating compared to my normal 60 minute workout.

All-or-nothing is the pattern under the pattern. 20 minutes on the road isn't cheating — it's maintenance, and maintenance is how you avoid the 3-month restart cycle. The goal during travel isn't progress, it's not losing ground. If you can show up at a reduced level consistently, you never have to rebuild from zero. That's actually a higher-leverage skill than the 60-minute workout.

title: Thinking about going back to school for an MBA

parts: I'm 29 and seriously considering an MBA. I have about 6 years of work experience in tech. I keep going back and forth — part of me thinks it's a great investment and part of me thinks it's an expensive piece of paper that my industry doesn't actually care about.

Both things can be true depending on what you want the MBA to do for you. What's the underlying goal — switching industries, accelerating into leadership, the network, or is it more a "something feels like it's missing" feeling?

Honestly a mix. I want to eventually start something but I feel like I don't know enough about the business side — finance, strategy, operations. I've always been on the product side and I feel like I have gaps. Also the network appeal is real — I know a few people from Harvard and Wharton and they seem to have access to things I don't.

The "I want to start something" framing changes the calculus. For entrepreneurship, an MBA is genuinely mixed — the network and the legitimacy signal are real, but the debt load ($200k+ for top programs) and 2 years out of the workforce are significant costs when you could be building instead. The business knowledge gaps you're describing can honestly be filled with a fraction of that investment — books, a finance course, finding a mentor. What would you build?

I've been thinking about something in the climate tech space — specifically tools for small businesses to measure and offset their carbon footprint. It feels early but it also feels important. My hesitation is I don't know the space well enough yet.

Climate tech for SMBs is genuinely interesting and it's a space where being early is an advantage not a liability. Rather than spending 2 years in an MBA to learn the space, you could spend the next 12 months going deep — talking to 50 small business owners about how they think about sustainability, working in the climate space, finding advisors. That knowledge is more valuable than a classroom version of it. The MBA might still make sense later, but not as a prerequisite to starting.

My best friend died 3 months ago. He was 33. It was sudden — a heart condition nobody knew about. I'm struggling more than I expected. I thought I'd be doing better by now and I feel like I'm failing at grief somehow.
I'm so sorry. Losing someone that young, that suddenly — there's no preparation for it and no right timeline for processing it. What makes you feel like you should be doing better by now?

I don't know. I think I have this idea that grief is supposed to move in some linear way and I'd slowly feel better. But I had a really good week last week and then yesterday I saw something that reminded me of him — a song he loved — and it completely wrecked me. I felt like I was back at day one.

The wave crashing back doesn't mean you're at day one — it means you loved him and the world keeps putting you in contact with that. Grief isn't linear, and the idea that it should be has made a lot of people feel like they're failing when they're actually just grieving. A song that wrecked you yesterday means it meant something. What was the song?

Landslide by Fleetwood Mac. He played it for me once on a long drive and we talked for hours that night about getting older and what we were scared of. It's probably one of the best conversations I ever had with anyone.

That's a beautiful memory to carry. And it makes sense that the song is a portal back to him — not just to loss, but to who he was and what you had. Those long-drive conversations where you say things you don't usually say are rare. You're not failing at grief. You're grieving someone who mattered enormously to you.
